section.title: Description
section.para: The Apache OpenNLP library is a machine learning based toolkit for the processing of natural language text. It supports the most common NLP tasks, such as tokenization, sentence segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, named entity extraction, chunking, parsing, coreference resolution, and sentiment analysis. These tasks are usually required to build more advanced text processing services. OpenNLP also includes maximum entropy and perceptron based machine learning.

The goal of the OpenNLP project will be to create a mature toolkit for the aforementioned tasks. An additional goal is to provide a large number of pre-built models for a variety of languages, as well as the annotated text resources that those models are derived from.

section.title: General Library Structure
section.para: The Apache OpenNLP library contains several components, enabling one to build a full natural language processing pipeline. These components include: sentence detector, tokenizer, name finder, document categorizer, sentiment analyzer, part-of-speech tagger, chunker, parser, coreference resolution. Components contain parts which enable one to execute the respective natural language processing task, to train a model and often also to evaluate a model. Each of these facilities is accessible via its application program interface (API). In addition, a command line interface (CLI) is provided for convenience of experiments and training.

section.title: Application Program Interface (API)
section.para: OpenNLP components have similar APIs. Normally, to execute a task, one should provide a model and an input.

section.title: Generic Example
Description
section.para: OpenNLP provides a command line script, serving as a unique entry point to all included tools. The script is located in the bin directory of OpenNLP binary distribution. Included are versions for Windows: opennlp.bat and Linux or compatible systems: opennlp.

section.title: List of tools
section.para: The list of command line tools for Apache OpenNLP , as well as a description of its arguments, is available at section .

section.title: Setting up
section.para: OpenNLP script uses JAVA_CMD and JAVA_HOME variables to determine which command to use to execute Java virtual machine.

OpenNLP script uses OPENNLP_HOME variable to determine the location of the binary distribution of OpenNLP. It is recommended to point this variable to the binary distribution of current OpenNLP version and update PATH variable to include $OPENNLP_HOME/bin or %OPENNLP_HOME%\bin.
Such configuration allows calling OpenNLP conveniently. Examples below suppose this configuration has been done.

section.title: Generic Example
section.para:
Apache OpenNLP provides a common command line script to access all its tools:
$ opennlp
This script prints current version of the library and lists all available tools:
OpenNLP <VERSION>. Usage: opennlp TOOL where TOOL is one of: Doccat learnable document categorizer DoccatTrainer trainer for the learnable document categorizer DoccatConverter converts leipzig data format to native OpenNLP format DictionaryBuilder builds a new dictionary SimpleTokenizer character class tokenizer TokenizerME learnable tokenizer TokenizerTrainer trainer for the learnable tokenizer TokenizerMEEvaluator evaluator for the learnable tokenizer TokenizerCrossValidator K-fold cross validator for the learnable tokenizer TokenizerConverter converts foreign data formats (namefinder,conllx,pos) to native OpenNLP format DictionaryDetokenizer SentenceDetector learnable sentence detector SentenceDetectorTrainer trainer for the learnable sentence detector SentenceDetectorEvaluator evaluator for the learnable sentence detector SentenceDetectorCrossValidator K-fold cross validator for the learnable sentence detector SentenceDetectorConverter converts foreign data formats (namefinder,conllx,pos) to native OpenNLP format TokenNameFinder learnable name finder TokenNameFinderTrainer trainer for the learnable name finder TokenNameFinderEvaluator Measures the performance of the NameFinder model with the reference data TokenNameFinderCrossValidator K-fold cross validator for the learnable Name Finder TokenNameFinderConverter converts foreign data formats (bionlp2004,conll03,conll02,ad) to native OpenNLP format CensusDictionaryCreator Converts 1990 US Census names into a dictionary POSTagger learnable part of speech tagger POSTaggerTrainer trains a model for the part-of-speech tagger POSTaggerEvaluator Measures the performance of the POS tagger model with the reference data POSTaggerCrossValidator K-fold cross validator for the learnable POS tagger POSTaggerConverter converts conllx data format to native OpenNLP format ChunkerME learnable chunker ChunkerTrainerME trainer for the learnable chunker ChunkerEvaluator Measures the performance of the Chunker model with the reference data ChunkerCrossValidator K-fold cross validator for the chunker ChunkerConverter converts ad data format to native OpenNLP format Parser performs full syntactic parsing ParserTrainer trains the learnable parser ParserEvaluator Measures the performance of the Parser model with the reference data BuildModelUpdater trains and updates the build model in a parser model CheckModelUpdater trains and updates the check model in a parser model TaggerModelReplacer replaces the tagger model in a parser model All tools print help when invoked with help parameter Example: opennlp SimpleTokenizer help

OpenNLP tools have similar command line structure and options. To discover tool options, run it with no parameters:
$ opennlp ToolName
The tool will output two blocks of help.

The first block describes the general structure of this tool command line:
Usage: opennlp TokenizerTrainer[.namefinder|.conllx|.pos] [-abbDict path] ... -model modelFile ...
The general structure of this tool command line includes the obligatory tool name (TokenizerTrainer), the optional format parameters ([.namefinder|.conllx|.pos]), the optional parameters ([-abbDict path] ...), and the obligatory parameters (-model modelFile ...).

The format parameters enable direct processing of non-native data without conversion. Each format might have its own parameters, which are displayed if the tool is executed without or with help parameter:
$ opennlp TokenizerTrainer.conllx help
Usage: opennlp TokenizerTrainer.conllx [-abbDict path] [-alphaNumOpt isAlphaNumOpt] ...
Arguments description: -abbDict path abbreviation dictionary in XML format. ...
To switch the tool to a specific format, add a dot and the format name after the tool name:
$ opennlp TokenizerTrainer.conllx -model en-pos.bin ...

The second block of the help message describes the individual arguments:
Arguments description: -type maxent|perceptron|perceptron_sequence The type of the token name finder model. One of maxent|perceptron|perceptron_sequence. -dict dictionaryPath The XML tag dictionary file ...

Most tools for processing need to be provided at least a model:
$ opennlp ToolName lang-model-name.bin
When tool is executed this way, the model is loaded and the tool is waiting for the input from standard input. This input is processed and printed to standard output.

Alternative, or one should say, most commonly used way is to use console input and output redirection options to provide also an input and an output files:
$ opennlp ToolName lang-model-name.bin < input.txt > output.txt
Most tools for model training need to be provided first a model name, optionally some training options (such as model type, number of iterations), and then the data.
A model name is just a file name.

Training options often include number of iterations, cutoff, abbreviations dictionary or something else. Sometimes it is possible to provide these options via training options file. In this case these options are ignored and the ones from the file are used.
For the data one has to specify the location of the data (filename) and often language and encoding.

A generic example of a command line to launch a tool trainer might be:
$ opennlp ToolNameTrainer -model en-model-name.bin -lang en -data input.train -encoding UTF-8
or with a format:
$ opennlp ToolNameTrainer.conll03 -model en-model-name.bin -lang en -data input.train \ -types per -encoding UTF-8

Most tools for model evaluation are similar to those for task execution, and need to be provided fist a model name, optionally some evaluation options (such as whether to print misclassified samples), and then the test data. A generic example of a command line to launch an evaluation tool might be:
$ opennlp ToolNameEvaluator -model en-model-name.bin -lang en -data input.test -encoding UTF-8

section.title: OpenNLP Models
section.para: OpenNLP supports training NLP models that can be used by OpenNLP. In this documentation we will refer to these models as "OpenNLP models." All NLP components of OpenNLP support this type of model. The sections below in this documentation describe how to train and use these models. Pre-trained models are available for some languages and some OpenNLP components.

section.title: ONNX Models
section.para: OpenNLP supports ONNX models via the ONNX Runtime for the Name Finder and Document Categorizer. This allows models trained by other frameworks such as PyTorch and Tensorflow to be used by OpenNLP. The documentation for each of the OpenNLP components that supports ONNX models describes how to use ONNX models for inference. DL inference uses Unicode-aware text chunking and optional input normalization; see .

note.para: OpenNLP does not support training models that can be used by the ONNX Runtime - ONNX models must be created outside OpenNLP using other tools.

section.title: Closing and resetting input streams
section.para: Close corpus streams after use, preferably with try-with-resources. Since 3.0.0, PlainTextByLineStream.reset() closes the reader from the previous pass before asking its InputStreamFactory for a new stream. The factory must therefore provide a fresh, readable stream for each pass, rather than return the stream that has just been closed.

The markable file stream that the command line tools and the format converters open for corpus files releases its file handle on close, including when closed through a wrapping reader. The Leipzig language-sample reader also closes the stream used to count source lines. These fixes prevent file handles from accumulating during repeated reads and training passes.

section.title: String Interning
section.para: OpenNLP provides different implementations for String interning to reduce memory footprint. By default, OpenNLP uses a custom String interner implementation.

Users may override by setting the following system property:
-Dopennlp.interner.class=opennlp.tools.util.jvm.JvmStringInterner
In addition, users can provide custom String interner implementations by implementing the interface 'StringInterner' and specify this class via 'opennlp.interner.class'.

section.title: Whitespace Definition
section.para: What counts as whitespace is a common interoperability gap across programming languages and libraries. The Unicode Character Database defines a binary White_Space property. As documented on Wikipedia's whitespace character page, Unicode defines exactly twenty-five characters with White_Space=yes (WSpace=Y / WS), including ordinary space and tab, the next-line control (U+0085), no-break and typographic spaces such as U+00A0 and U+2007, and the line and paragraph separators (U+2028/U+2029). That page also states the cross-language weakness directly: Most languages only recognize whitespace characters that have an ASCII code. They disallow most or all of the Unicode codes listed above. Java is a concrete example of that mismatch: Character.isWhitespace omits the no-break spaces and U+0085 while including the information separators U+001C..U+001F, and Java's default \s regex class is likewise an ASCII-oriented subset unless Unicode character-class mode is enabled. Text extracted from PDFs, HTML, and word processors regularly carries the wider set, so a tokenizer that follows the JVM predicate and one that follows Unicode will disagree on those documents.

Tokenization, corpus format parsing, and feature generation therefore classify whitespace using the Unicode White_Space property by default, via StringUtil.isWhitespace and the related StringUtil.splitOnUnicodeWhitespace / trimUnicodeWhitespace helpers (code-point scans, not regular expressions). Models trained with OpenNLP 1.x or 2.x used the legacy definition (the union of Character.isWhitespace and the Unicode Zs category). As of this release, that covers all published OpenNLP models, so set the property below when decoding those models if you need byte-identical tokenization at the few code points where the two definitions differ.

Users may switch to the legacy definition by setting the following system property:
-Dopennlp.whitespace.mode=LEGACY

Accepted values are LEGACY and UNICODE (the default), case-insensitive; any other value throws an IllegalArgumentException. The setting applies process-wide, so training and decoding of a given model must use the same value. Legacy support is scheduled for removal in 4.0.

section.title: Service providers
section.para: OpenNLP has two ways to reach an implementation that core does not know. ExtensionLoader instantiates a class whose name comes from a model manifest, an XML descriptor or a training parameter, so the caller must already know that name. The provider SPI in opennlp.tools.util.ext works the other way around: a jar on the class path announces what it can do, and OpenNLP picks an implementation for the request at hand. It is meant for optional implementations that ship separately, such as an annotator, a stemmer or an embedder.

Each service interface has a provider interface of its own that extends Provider, for example DocumentAnnotatorProvider extends Provider<DocumentAnnotator>. An implementation needs a public no-argument constructor and is listed in META-INF/services/ under the fully qualified name of that provider interface, the usual java.util.ServiceLoader layout. A provider states its name(), a priority(), whether it isAvailable() in the running process, for example whether an optional dependency is present, and whether it supports a request. The request is a ProviderSpec: an optional location, such as a model file, and string options. Neither the constructor nor the static initializer, the availability check or supports may load a model or initialize a native library, because they run while the candidates are collected, before one of them is chosen.

Providers.of scans the class path once, so an application creates its instance at startup and keeps it, rather than resolving per request. The instance is immutable and thread-safe. Keep it in a field owned by the application, for example a servlet context attribute or an application scoped bean; a static field is wrong when OpenNLP is deployed in a class loader shared by several applications, because it would keep one application's providers and their class loader alive. The lookup uses the thread context class loader when that loader sees the provider interface, and the class loader of the provider interface otherwise. On a thread whose context class loader is not the application's, such as a thread of a pool, only the providers of the provider interface's own class loader are found, so a library or a framework integration captures the class loader at startup and passes it to Providers.of(spi, loader). Resolving is not free either: keep what select returned instead of resolving per request, and keep in mind that a provider blocking in isAvailable() or supports() blocks every resolution of that provider interface.

select returns the available provider with the highest priority that supports the request. If several share the highest priority, an AmbiguousProviderException names them; if none supports the request, an UnsatisfiedProviderException names the installed providers. supporting returns every matching provider, best first, and byName resolves one by name. Providers may share a name, in which case the higher priority wins, which is how a module replaces the provider of another module. What create returns belongs to the caller, who also closes it if it is closeable.

Three keys configure resolution, all named after the provider interface. opennlp.provider.<interface> selects a provider by name, for example opennlp.provider.opennlp.tools.document.DocumentAnnotatorProvider=stemmer. It narrows the providers that support the request, so a selected provider that does not support the request is reported as unsatisfied rather than used. opennlp.provider.<interface>.disabled holds a comma separated list of provider names and provider class names that are not resolved; a name stays listed by installed(), while a class name is never instantiated, which keeps a provider out of the process entirely and therefore has to be configured before the providers are looked up. The third key, opennlp.provider.<interface>.allowed, is described below. The first two are read from META-INF/opennlp/providers.properties, encoded in UTF-8, of the class loader the providers were looked up with; where several files carry the same key, the one with the highest configuration.ordinal wins, and a system property of the same name wins over all files. In a native image the file is read only when it is registered as a resource.

Adding a jar to the class path is a decision to trust its code: every provider of the provider interface is instantiated when the providers are looked up, and any jar can carry a providers.properties that selects or disables a provider, which OpenNLP logs with the file it came from. Providers may also share a name, so a name is a convenient handle and not a guarantee of which implementation answers. An application that must not be reconfigured by a library on its class path passes its own source, which is also how two deployments in one application server configure themselves independently: Providers.of(spi, loader, key -> myConfiguration.get(key)).

An operator who wants to decide which implementations may run at all uses opennlp.provider.<interface>.allowed, a comma separated list of provider class names and of package prefixes, which have to end with a dot. Only those classes are instantiated, every other provider of that interface is left out whatever it is named, an unset or blank value allows all of them and a value that holds only separators allows none. It is read from a system property or from the source an application passes, never from a providers.properties that any jar could carry, and it is checked before a provider class is instantiated, so it has to be configured before the providers are looked up. A provider left out this way is counted in the message of an UnsatisfiedProviderException together with the key.

What the allowed key decides is which class names may be instantiated, not where their code comes from. Two jars can carry the same class name, and which one is loaded is the class loader's decision, so a package prefix widens that further. A provider name is weaker still: names may be shared between jars, so opennlp.provider.<interface> is a convenience for choosing between implementations, not a security control.
Where the origin of an implementation matters, decide by the class instead of by its name:

The predicate is asked for every provider class the configuration keys leave, before an instance of it is created, and it can look at the code source, the module or the signers of the class. The class is loaded and linked before it is asked, including whatever a custom class loader does while loading it, but it is not initialized: a rejected provider runs neither its static initializer nor its constructor, and is counted among the skipped ones. The predicate must therefore not initialize the class itself, for instance by reading a static field, and must be deterministic, thread-safe and free of blocking calls. A predicate that throws ends the lookup, so a failure never widens the policy. The strongest boundary remains the class path itself: look the providers up with a class loader that sees only the jars you trust. The lookup also logs at debug level which location each provider class was loaded from, for auditing.

A provider that cannot be loaded, whose name is unusable, or that throws from name() or priority() is skipped while the providers are looked up, so one broken jar does not hide the others, and the number of skipped providers appears in the message of an UnsatisfiedProviderException. A provider that throws from isAvailable() or supports() is left out of that one resolution instead. Both are reported once per provider and method as a warning and at debug level afterwards. A configuration file that cannot be read, and a class loader that cannot list its files at all, fail the lookup with a ProviderResolutionException. Discovery works on the class path; OpenNLP declares no JPMS provides directives for the module path.

The runtime registers one provider, stemmer, which creates a StemmerAnnotator for a request without location whose only option is algorithm: porter, which is also the default when the option is absent, for the Porter stemmer, or the name of a Snowball algorithm.
